reading.rtitle: Inside Sucafina Santos -- The Traceability Project
paras: THE START. Since March, a small team in the Santos office has been working on a new traceability system. The goal is simple: a buyer in Seattle or Hamburg should know exactly which farm every bag of coffee came from. To get the ball rolling, the team touched base with forty growers in Minas Gerais in the first two weeks.

THE PROBLEM. The first plan used an expensive app, and many small farms did not have good internet. After a month of tests, the director said: back to the drawing board. Nobody wanted to cut corners on quality, so the team had to think outside the box.

THE NEW PLAN. Since June, the team has been testing a simpler system with paper codes and one phone per cooperative. A new analyst joined in July and hit the ground running: in his first week, he trained six cooperatives.

WHAT IT MEANS. The growers get better prices, and the buyers get the information they have been asking for. It is a win-win, and it keeps the company ahead of the curve. The team has been keeping the director in the loop every Friday, and the full launch is planned for next year.
reading.source: Newsletter article written for this lesson. The project and the people are fictional.

listenings.text: Many of my clients are international professionals, and they all tell me the same thing. In meetings, they understand every word, but they do not understand the sentence. Someone says, let's touch base next week, or it's back to the drawing board, and they get lost. The reason is simple: the meaning of an idiom is not in the words. If you translate it word by word, it does not work. So here is how I teach them. Do not learn idioms from a list. Learn them in context. When you hear one in a meeting or a podcast, write down the whole sentence, and who said it, and why. After a few weeks, you will start to use them naturally. And one warning: do not use too many. One or two idioms in a meeting sound natural and confident. Ten idioms in five minutes sound strange, like you are reading from a book.

In my first year in London, I worked for a coffee trader near the river. One evening, after a long meeting, my manager looked at the clock and said, okay, let's call it a day. I did not understand. I thought he wanted to give the day a name, or maybe end the whole project. I was really worried. The next morning, everybody was back at work, and a colleague laughed and explained it to me. It just meant: let's stop working for today. That night, I started a notebook. Every time I heard an expression in a meeting, I wrote down the whole sentence. I have been keeping that notebook for six years now, and I have been adding new expressions since my first week. Today I use some of them myself, and nobody in the office thinks about where I am from.

extra_audio.text: Our team has been working on the traceability project since March. First, we touched base with forty growers to get the ball rolling. Our first plan was too expensive, so we went back to the drawing board. Since then, we have been testing a simpler system with ten farms. The new system is a win-win for the growers and for our buyers. I will keep you in the loop about the results next month.
